draft_ledger.reference_answer:
Across the available studies, several distinct groups of factors make it difficult to directly compare PFAS adsorption performance between granular activated carbon (GAC) and ion‑exchange (IEX) resins, even when similar PFAS are considered.

From a study‑design and operating‑condition perspective, performance is clearly matrix‑dependent. Riegel et al. evaluated activated carbon filtration and ion‑exchange treatment in a specific PFAS‑polluted groundwater matrix, reporting that short‑chain PFCA (PFBA, PFPeA) were only sufficiently removed over relatively short run times of 6000 and 11,000 bed volumes (BV) with activated carbon, and that ion‑exchange media removed short‑chain PFCA over relatively short run times of 5000 BV for PFBA, 10,000 BV for PFPeA, and 18,000 BV for PFHxA in that same matrix.
This underscores that observed run times and breakthrough behaviors are tied to the groundwater matrix used and cannot automatically be transferred to other waters without adjustment.

Ion‑exchange performance is additionally sensitive to the presence of background species typical of natural waters. Shaikh and co‑workers note that commercially available ion‑exchange resins, though widely used for PFAS, can have their performance “significantly compromised in the presence of background species commonly found in natural water matrices, including multivalent cations, anions, and dissolved organic matter,” with these species (present at mg L−1 levels) competing with trace‑level PFAS for active sites and in some cases contributing to pore blockage, which diminishes resin capacity and kinetics.
Thus, comparing IEX performance across studies without aligning matrix composition is misleading.

The way experiments are run and metrics are defined also varies. In the same Riegel study, PFAS sorption on both activated carbon and IEX was characterized in equilibrium batch experiments with demineralized water using Freundlich isotherm parameters (KF and n), while in the groundwater column tests performance was described by run time and bed volumes to achieve sufficient removal.
Sorption isotherms and solid‑phase concentrations were used to interpret resin affinity in another part of that work, and bed‑volume run times were again the key metric in the column filters.
Because some studies report isotherm parameters, others emphasize solid‑phase loadings, and still others focus on BV run times or breakthrough curves, it is difficult to directly compare numerical performance between GAC and IEX unless the same operating modes and endpoints are used.

Beyond design and matrix issues, PFAS‑ and adsorbent‑specific factors strongly shape observed performance and complicate cross‑material comparisons.
Mechanistically, Sanzana et al. report that PFAS adsorption on GAC “primarily involve[s] hydrophobic interactions with the pore surfaces of the carbon,” supplemented by secondary electrostatic interactions that can attract or repel PFAS depending on the GAC surface charge.
Riegel et al. describe a different mechanism for anion‑exchange resins, where the sorption of PFAS is “a mixture of anion exchange and physical sorption, like van der Waals interaction … that might be less dependent on substance polarity.”
Because GAC emphasizes hydrophobic interactions and surface charge effects, while IEX combines electrostatic exchange with less polarity‑dependent physical sorption, the same PFAS can interact differently with each adsorbent type under the same nominal conditions, making simple performance rankings misleading.

Within any given study, PFAS chain length and functional group are major determinants of adsorption affinity for both material classes.
In equilibrium experiments with activated carbon, Riegel et al. found the sorption order PFOA > PFHxA > PFPeA > PFBA, indicating that longer‑chain PFCA sorb more strongly than shorter ones under those conditions.

They further noted that, across all adsorbents tested (including both activated carbon and IEX), short‑chain PFCA had significantly lower sorption affinity than long‑chain PFAS or short‑chain PFSA.

Across the cited studies, several regeneration approaches for PFAS-loaded ion-exchange resins and their limitations are described.

For PS-DVB anion-exchange resins used in drinking-water treatment, Liu and Sun evaluated chloride-based brines as regenerants. They note that, because “using high percentages of organic solvents is challenging in full-scale water treatment, using 10% simple chloride salts without organic solvents might be the most reasonable option for regenerating PFAS-loaded PS-DVB resins.” In their tests on five PS-DVB resins (including macroporous and gel-type materials), regeneration with chloride brine at this strength was identified as an optimal salt condition. Comparison of different anions showed that “chloride salts worked the best for our five tested PS-DVB resins, followed by bicarbonate and … acetate salts,” and they conclude that bicarbonate, though more eco‑friendly and effective for nitrate-laden resins, “is not suitable for PFAS treatment by PS-DVB resins.” They also examined the influence of pH and base addition by partially replacing NH4Cl or NaCl with NaOH, and observed that “our results indicate that NaOH is a weaker regenerant than NH4Cl or NaCl to recover PFAS.”

Despite optimizing brine composition in this way, regeneration performance was limited for many resin–PFAS combinations. Using 10% brine, “The two gel-type resins, PFA694E and DOWEX1, show < 50% recovery for almost all PFAS, especially for the PFAS-specific PFA694E, which had the lowest recovery (< 25%).” The authors further conclude that “resin regeneration for drinking water treatment might be limited for most PFAS except short-chain PFCA and PFECA,” and they classify PFAS-specific resins as essentially non-regenerable by standard methods: “the PFAS-specific resins are non-regenerable in our study via the conventional regeneration approaches, consistent with the manufacturer’s recommendation of one-time use.”

Recognizing that “simple salt solutions do not effectively release PFAS from resins, and it is not practical to regenerate resins every cycle with organic solvents,” Liu and Sun propose an operational compromise. They suggest that “a more practical operation is to regenerate resins with simple salt solutions to release other components in water (major anions, natural organic matter) adsorbed together with PFAS to release these sites for PFAS uptake in the following round of application.” In this view, simple brines would mainly clear competing anions and natural organic matter between cycles, with organic-solvent regeneration, if used, applied more sparingly.

Other work summarized by Aumeier et al. highlights solvent-containing regenerants. Riegel et al. “could elute a wide range of PFAS from a loaded anion exchange resin using mixtures of ethanol and NaOH or HCl, reaching satisfactory desorption with only 3 to 10 bed volumes of regeneration solution.” Thus, mixtures of ethanol with NaOH or HCl represent an effective regeneration protocol for PFAS-loaded anion-exchange resins, achieving substantial desorption within a modest number of bed volumes.

However, these advantages are tempered by operational constraints. Aumeier et al. note that “due to the challenges in preventing solvent leaching during reuse and increased efforts for solvent/brine treatment such resins are mainly used in a single-use-and-dispose mode in water treatment so far.” More broadly, Sanzana et al. remark that “although aqueous or solvent-based techniques can be used to regenerate some resins, the waste streams produced are dangerous, expensive to handle, and often incompatible with the treatment processes that produced them,” underscoring the waste-management challenges associated with both aqueous and solvent-based regeneration.

Additional limitations and knowledge gaps are identified at the technology level. Aumeier et al. state that “while anion exchange resins have advantages compared to AC in terms of removal performance of short-chain PFAS anions, knowledge gaps exist in the optimal selection of resins in terms of minimizing negative impact and fouling by natural organic matter as well as regeneration options.” Coupled with Sanzana et al.’s statement that waste streams from aqueous or solvent-based regeneration “are dangerous, expensive to handle, and often incompatible” with the originating processes, this indicates that resin choice, fouling behavior, and downstream handling of regenerant waste are still significant open questions for practical deployment.

Beyond salts and conventional solvent mixtures, other regeneration strategies have been explored. Zheng et al. report that “cationic cetyltrimethylammonium bromide (CTAB) enabled the efficient desorption of PFOS from saturated ion-exchange resins (IERs), providing a practical regeneration strategy.” Importantly for reuse, “The regenerated IERs retained their adsorption efficiency over at least five reuse cycles.” This illustrates a surfactant-assisted desorption approach in which CTAB regeneration maintains resin performance over multiple cycles.

Across these studies, the evidence stresses that regeneration behavior is resin- and PFAS-specific. In Liu and Sun’s work, “PFAS-specific resins are non-regenerable … via the conventional regeneration approaches,” and they also observe that “simple salt solutions do not effectively release PFAS from resins.” As such, while various regenerants (simple chloride brines, solvent-containing mixtures such as ethanol with NaOH or HCl, and CTAB) have been reported or proposed, their practical usefulness is constrained by PFAS chemistry and chain length, resin structure and functionality, solvent-handling and waste-management requirements, and the still-incomplete understanding of optimal regeneration strategies.

draft_ledger.reference_answer:
Across the available membrane PFAS studies, one key limitation for cross-study comparison is that some work uses natural raw water while many other studies do not. In the natural raw water study, the authors explicitly state that, 

"Other studies have not used natural raw water as was done in this study, which hampers direct comparisons."

This means that the raw water matrix itself differs from the simpler or synthetic matrices used elsewhere, so differences in PFAS removal cannot be cleanly attributed to the membrane alone.

A second complicating feature of natural or real-world matrices is the presence of many other contaminants. In a study on PFAS removal from real wastewater, the matrix contained 

"11 pollutants that compete for adsorption or rejection by the membrane. This competition can reduce the efficiency of the membrane for PFAS removal compared to simpler matrices."

Thus, in complex natural or wastewater matrices, multiple co-pollutants vie for adsorption or rejection at the membrane, so observed PFAS removals can be lower than in cleaner, simpler feed waters, making direct comparison across matrices uncertain. These findings should be interpreted as study-specific limitations on comparability, not as universal rules for all membranes, PFAS, or water types. The available evidence does not provide approved detail on how individual small PFAS behave differently in natural raw water versus simpler matrices, so such behavior cannot be specified beyond noting that matrix differences hamper comparisons.
